key: It is a weighted average of the masses of the element's natural isotopes.
wrong: Some atoms have part of a proton.
Atoms constantly gain and lose neutrons.
It is the mass number rounded to two decimal places.
explanation: The atomic mass is a weighted average over the element's natural isotopes, each counted by its percent abundance. No single atom has the average mass.

q: Thallium has two natural isotopes, thallium-203 and thallium-205. Its average atomic mass is 204.38 amu. Which isotope is more abundant?
wrong: It cannot be told without a calculation.
explanation: Halfway between 203 and 205 is about 204. The average, 204.38, is closer to 205, so thallium-205 is more abundant (about 70% of natural thallium).

q: Boron is a micronutrient that almond trees need. Natural boron is 19.9% boron-10 (10.0129 amu) and 80.1% boron-11 (11.0093 amu). What is boron's average atomic mass?
explanation: (0.199)(10.0129 amu) + (0.801)(11.0093 amu) = 1.99 + 8.82 = 10.81 amu. Check: it lies between the two masses, closer to boron-11, the more abundant isotope.

q: Potassium is a key nutrient in Central Valley soils and almond hulls. Natural potassium is almost all potassium-39 (38.964 amu, 93.26%) and potassium-41 (40.962 amu, 6.73%). Using these two isotopes, what is potassium's average atomic mass?
explanation: (0.9326)(38.964) + (0.0673)(40.962) = 36.3378 + 2.7567 = 39.09 amu, close to 39 because potassium-39 dominates. The abundances add to 99.99% because a tiny amount of potassium-40 (about 0.01%) is left out; including it brings the value to the periodic table's 39.098 amu.

q: Silver, used in some dental alloys, is 51.84% silver-107 (106.905 amu) and 48.16% silver-109 (108.905 amu). What is the average atomic mass of silver?
explanation: (0.5184)(106.905 amu) + (0.4816)(108.905 amu) = 55.42 + 52.45 = 107.87 amu. Silver-107 is slightly more abundant, so the answer sits just below the halfway value of 107.905.

q: Neon has three natural isotopes. Use the data to calculate neon's average atomic mass.
A student calculates the average atomic mass of copper from its two isotopes (62.93 amu and 64.93 amu) and gets 6355 amu. What is the most likely mistake?
key: Multiplying by the percent abundances instead of the fractional abundances
wrong: Taking a simple average instead of a weighted average
Swapping the abundances of the two isotopes
explanation: Any average must lie between the isotope masses. 6355 is 100 times too big, the sign of using percents (69.15, 30.85) instead of fractions (0.6915, 0.3085). The correct answer is 63.55 amu.

q: An element has two isotopes with masses 20.0 amu and 22.0 amu. Which value could be its average atomic mass?
explanation: Any weighted average lies between 20.0 and 22.0 amu, so only 20.2 amu is possible. It would mean the lighter isotope is far more abundant.

q: Nitrogen is a major fertilizer element. Use the isotope data in the table to calculate nitrogen's average atomic mass.
explanation: (0.9964)(14.003) + (0.0036)(15.000) = 13.953 + 0.054 = 14.01 amu, very close to 14 because nitrogen-14 is 99.64% of natural nitrogen.

q: Carbon's average atomic mass is 12.011 amu. Which statement about a single carbon atom in a breath sample is true?
key: Its mass is close to 12.000 amu or to 13.003 amu, depending on which isotope it is.
wrong: Its mass is exactly 12.011 amu, like every carbon atom.
It is most likely carbon-13, since 12.011 is more than 12.
explanation: The 12.011 amu value is an average over a mixture that is about 99% carbon-12 and 1% carbon-13. Any one atom has the mass of its own isotope: about 12.000 or 13.003 amu.

q: On a drawing of a light wave, what does the wavelength measure?
key: The distance from one peak of the wave to the next peak
wrong: The number of peaks that pass a point each second
The height of a peak above the middle line of the wave
The speed at which the wave travels
explanation: The wavelength, λ, is the distance from one peak to the next. The frequency, ν, counts peaks per second. They are tied together by c = λν.

q: Light of one color is replaced by light whose wavelength is twice as long. What happens to the frequency?
wrong: It stays the same, because the speed of light does not change.
explanation: Because λν = c is constant, doubling λ means ν is cut in half. Longer waves pass a point less often.

q: Some older street lamps in Valley towns glow yellow-orange because they contain sodium vapor, which gives off light at 589 nm. What is the frequency of this light?
explanation: 589 nm × (10−9 m / 1 nm) = 5.89 × 10−7 m. ν = c/λ = (3.00 × 108)/(5.89 × 10−7) = 5.09 × 1014 Hz (3 significant figures).

q: A 1.5-tesla MRI scanner sends radio-frequency pulses at 6.39 × 107 Hz. What is the wavelength of these radio waves?
explanation: λ = c/ν = (3.00 × 108 m s−1)/(6.39 × 107 s−1) = 4.69 m. Radio waves are the longest waves in the spectrum, so a wavelength of a few meters makes sense.

q: Germicidal UV-C light used to disinfect biosafety cabinets has a frequency of 1.18 × 1015 Hz. What is the energy of one photon of this light?
explanation: E = hν = (6.626 × 10−34 J s)(1.18 × 1015 s−1) = 7.82 × 10−19 J (3 significant figures, set by the frequency).

q: Newborn jaundice is often treated with phototherapy, blue light that the baby's skin absorbs. One phototherapy lamp uses LEDs that give off light at 455 nm. What is the energy of one photon of this light?
explanation: λ = 4.55 × 10−7 m. E = hc/λ = (6.626 × 10−34)(3.00 × 108)/(4.55 × 10−7) = 4.37 × 10−19 J. This is context only: the energy of one photon, not a dose.

q: Which list puts these regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in order of increasing photon energy?
explanation: From long wavelength to short: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma. Energy rises in the same order, so radio < infrared < ultraviolet < X-rays.

q: A pulse oximeter shines red light at 660 nm and infrared light at 940 nm through a fingertip. Which statement compares the two photons correctly?
key: The 660 nm photon has the higher frequency and the higher energy.
wrong: The 940 nm photon has the higher energy, because its wavelength is larger.
The 940 nm photon has the higher frequency, but the 660 nm photon has the higher energy.
Both photons have the same energy, because both travel at the speed of light.
explanation: Shorter wavelength means higher frequency (c = λν) and higher energy (E = hν). The 660 nm red photon has the higher frequency and energy, about 940/660 ≈ 1.4 times that of the infrared photon.

q: A dental assistant turns a curing light to a brighter setting without changing its color. What changes?
key: More photons come out each second; each photon has the same energy as before.
wrong: Each photon now has more energy.
The wavelength of the light gets shorter.
The frequency of the light goes up.
explanation: A brighter light sends out more photons, but each photon's energy depends only on its wavelength (E = hc/λ), which is unchanged because the color is the same.

q: Radiology staff wear dosimeters and lead aprons around X-ray equipment, but nobody worries about the radio waves from a cell phone in the same way. Why?
key: Each X-ray photon has enough energy to knock electrons out of atoms; each radio photon has far too little.
wrong: X-rays travel faster than radio waves.
Radio waves have shorter wavelengths, so they pass through the body without stopping.
Radio waves are not electromagnetic radiation.
explanation: X-rays and gamma rays are called ionizing radiation because each photon carries enough energy to knock electrons out of atoms. Radio photons have very long wavelengths and very low energies, too little to break bonds or ionize atoms.

q: A UV-C germicidal lamp gives off light at 254 nm, and a sodium lamp gives off light at 589 nm. About how many times more energy does one UV-C photon carry than one sodium-lamp photon?
explanation: EUV/ENa = (hc/254 nm)/(hc/589 nm) = 589/254 = 2.32. Shorter wavelength, more energy: each UV-C photon carries a bit more than twice the energy, enough to damage the DNA of microbes.

q: The table lists light used in four settings. Which photon has the lowest frequency?
key: Near-infrared light measured by an orchard-imaging drone
explanation: Because c = λν, the longest wavelength has the lowest frequency: near-infrared, 850 nm. In order of increasing frequency: 850 nm < 589 nm < 470 nm < 254 nm.

q: White light from a bulb passes through a prism and spreads into a smooth rainbow. Light from a hydrogen discharge tube shows only a few sharp colored lines. What are these two kinds of spectra called?
key: The rainbow is a continuous spectrum; the hydrogen lines are a line (emission) spectrum.
wrong: The rainbow is a line spectrum; the hydrogen lines are a continuous spectrum.
Both are continuous spectra, because both come from light.
Both are emission spectra, so they always look the same.
explanation: White light gives a continuous spectrum, every color with no gaps. A glowing gas such as hydrogen gives a line (emission) spectrum: only certain wavelengths, a pattern unique to that element.

q: In a hydrogen atom, which electron jump gives off a photon of light?
explanation: Emission happens when an electron drops to a lower level: n = 4 to n = 2 releases the energy difference as a photon (hydrogen's 486 nm blue-green line). Upward jumps absorb energy.

q: In hydrogen, the drop from n = 3 to n = 2 gives the red line at 656 nm, and the drop from n = 4 to n = 2 gives the blue-green line at 486 nm. Why does the n = 4 to n = 2 drop give the shorter wavelength?
key: It is a bigger energy drop, so its photon has more energy, and more energy means a shorter wavelength.
wrong: It is a smaller energy drop, and smaller drops give shorter wavelengths.
Electrons in higher levels move faster, so the light they give off moves faster.
Blue-green light is brighter than red light.
explanation: Falling from n = 4 to n = 2 is a bigger energy drop than n = 3 to n = 2. A bigger drop gives a higher-energy photon, and since E = hc/λ, a higher energy means a shorter wavelength: 486 nm instead of 656 nm.

q: A flame test turns a flame bright yellow-orange for sodium, red for strontium, and blue-green for copper. What does the Bohr model say causes each element's own colors?
key: Each element has its own set of fixed energy levels, so its electrons can drop only by certain amounts, giving only certain wavelengths.
wrong: Each element absorbs every wavelength equally and gives off the leftover colors.
The color depends only on how hot the flame is.
Electrons can have any energy, so each element picks a favorite color.
explanation: Heat excites the electrons; when they drop back, each drop releases a photon whose energy equals the gap. Because each element has its own fixed energy levels, it gives off its own set of wavelengths, like a bar code.

q: Which statement describes an atom in an excited state?
key: At least one electron has absorbed energy and is in a higher level than it would be in the ground state.
wrong: All of its electrons are in the lowest energy levels available.
It has lost an electron and become a positive ion.
Its electrons sit between two energy levels.
explanation: In the excited state, an electron has absorbed energy and jumped to a higher level. It soon drops back to the ground state and gives off the energy difference as a photon.

q: Which statement about the Bohr model is true?
key: It explains hydrogen's line spectrum well, but it does not work for atoms with more than one electron.
wrong: It describes electrons as clouds called orbitals.
It says electrons can have any amount of energy.
It was replaced because it could not explain hydrogen's spectrum.
explanation: The Bohr model's quantized energy levels explain hydrogen's lines, and that central idea is still correct. But it fails for atoms with more than one electron, and electrons do not move in neat orbits; the quantum-mechanical model, with orbitals, replaced it.

q: Hydrogen's blue-green line has a wavelength of 486 nm. What is the energy of one photon of this light?
explanation: E = hc/λ = (6.626 × 10−34)(3.00 × 108)/(4.86 × 10−7) = 4.09 × 10−19 J, the energy gap between hydrogen's n = 4 and n = 2 levels.

q: A sodium street lamp gives off mostly yellow-orange light near 589 nm instead of a full rainbow. What does this tell you?
key: Sodium's electrons can drop only between certain energy levels, so only certain wavelengths are given off.
wrong: Sodium atoms absorb all colors except yellow-orange.
The lamp's glass filters out the other colors.
Yellow-orange light has the most energy of all visible colors.
explanation: Sodium's electrons have only certain allowed energies, so only certain drops, and therefore only certain wavelengths, are possible. Its strongest lines are yellow-orange, near 589 nm.

q: The table gives hydrogen's four visible emission lines. Each line comes from an electron dropping to n = 2. The 434 nm line comes from a drop from which level?
explanation: Bigger drop, shorter wavelength. 656 nm is n = 3 → 2 and 486 nm is n = 4 → 2, so 434 nm is n = 5 → 2 and 410 nm is n = 6 → 2.

q: What is the greatest number of electrons that one orbital can hold?
explanation: Each orbital holds at most 2 electrons, drawn as one up arrow and one down arrow (↑↓). Subshells hold more only because they contain more orbitals.

q: How many orbitals are in a p subshell, and how many electrons can the subshell hold?
explanation: The p subshell has 3 orbitals, each holding 2 electrons, so it holds 6 electrons. That is also why the p block of the periodic table is 6 columns wide.

q: How many electrons can the fourth shell (n = 4) hold in all?
explanation: Shell 4 has four subshells: 4s (2), 4p (6), 4d (10) and 4f (14). Total = 32 electrons (2n2 with n = 4).

q: Which description matches the shapes of s and p orbitals?
key: An s orbital is a sphere around the nucleus; a p orbital has two lobes on opposite sides of the nucleus.
wrong: An s orbital has two lobes; a p orbital is a sphere.
Both are spheres, but p orbitals are larger.
Both are flat circles, like the orbits in the Bohr model.
explanation: An s orbital is a sphere centered on the nucleus (a 2s sphere is bigger than a 1s). A p orbital has two lobes, like a dumbbell, and the three p orbitals point along three perpendicular directions.

q: A student draws the 2p subshell of a nitrogen atom as 2p [↑↓][↑][  ]. Which rule is broken?
wrong: No rule is broken; the diagram is correct.
explanation: In equal-energy orbitals, electrons go one per orbital with the same spin before any pair up (Hund's rule), like passengers taking empty bus seats first. Nitrogen's 2p is [↑][↑][↑], with 3 unpaired electrons.

q: Which orbital box breaks the Pauli exclusion principle?
explanation: The Pauli exclusion principle allows at most two electrons per orbital, with opposite spins. [↑↑] puts two same-spin electrons in one box, so it is not allowed.

q: Following the Aufbau principle, which subshell fills right after 3p?
explanation: Filling order: 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p 5s. That is why potassium and calcium, in row 4, put their last electrons in 4s before any 3d electrons appear.

q: The orbital diagram shows a neutral atom in its ground state. Which element is it?
explanation: Arrows: 1s (2), 2s (2), 2p (6), 3s (2), 3p (2) = 14 electrons. Z = 14 is silicon. The two 3p electrons are in separate orbitals with the same spin, as Hund's rule requires.

q: How many unpaired electrons does a ground-state oxygen atom have?
explanation: O has 8 electrons: 1s [↑↓] 2s [↑↓] 2p [↑↓][↑][↑]. Count the single arrows: 2 unpaired electrons.

q: Which diagram correctly shows the valence subshells (3s and 3p) of a ground-state silicon atom?
explanation: Si is [Ne] 3s2 3p2. Fill 3s with a pair (Pauli), then put the two 3p electrons in different orbitals with the same spin (Hund): 3s [↑↓] 3p [↑][↑][  ].

q: A student drew this orbital diagram for a ground-state carbon atom. Which rule does it break?
wrong: It breaks no rule; it is the ground state of carbon.
explanation: The diagram shows 2s with one electron and 2p with three. In the ground state, 2s fills before 2p (Aufbau principle). Carbon's ground state is 1s2 2s2 2p2; the drawing is an excited state.

q: Magnesium ions are needed by hundreds of enzymes in the body. What is the full electron configuration of a magnesium atom?
explanation: Mg (Z = 12): 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2. Check: 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 = 12. Magnesium is in group 2, and every group 2 element ends in s2.

q: Potassium is a key electrolyte in nerve and heart cells. What is the full electron configuration of a potassium atom (Z = 19)?
explanation: K (19 electrons): 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s1. Check: 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 6 + 1 = 19. Group 1 elements all end in s1.

q: Calcium ions trigger muscle contraction. What is the noble-gas (shorthand) configuration of a calcium atom?
explanation: Ca (Z = 20) is in row 4, group 2. Argon ends row 3, so [Ar] 4s2. Check: 18 + 2 = 20.

q: Which element has the configuration [Ne] 3s2 3p4?
explanation: [Ne] = 10 electrons, plus 3s2 3p4 = 6 more: 16 electrons, so Z = 16, sulfur. The 3p tells you row 3, and p4 tells you the fourth column of the p block (group 16).

q: Iodide in iodized salt helps the thyroid gland make its hormones. What is the noble-gas configuration of an iodine atom (Z = 53)?
explanation: I is in row 5, group 17. After [Kr] (36 electrons), read across row 5: 5s2, 4d10, 5p5. [Kr] 5s2 4d10 5p5. Check: 36 + 2 + 10 + 5 = 53, and like every halogen it ends in s2 p5.

q: Arsenic, a contaminant in some Central Valley well water, is in row 4, group 15. Which subshell does arsenic's last electron enter?
explanation: Arsenic sits in the p block (groups 13 to 18) of row 4, so its last electron enters 4p: As is [Ar] 4s2 3d10 4p3.

q: What is the electron configuration of the potassium ion, K+?
explanation: K is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s1. Removing the 4s electron gives 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 (18 electrons), isoelectronic with argon.

q: What is the electron configuration of the nitride ion, N3−?
explanation: N is 1s2 2s2 2p3 (7 electrons). Adding 3 gives 1s2 2s2 2p6, 10 electrons, isoelectronic with neon.

q: Which electrolyte ion is isoelectronic with argon?
explanation: Isoelectronic means same number of electrons (same configuration). Argon has 18. Ca2+: 20 − 2 = 18, so Ca2+. Na+, Mg2+ and F− each have 10, like neon.

q: A student writes 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p3 for selenium (Z = 34). What is wrong?
key: It has one electron too few: the superscripts add to 33, which is arsenic. Selenium ends in 4p4.
wrong: The d block in row 4 should be written as 4d.
Nothing is wrong; it is the correct configuration of selenium.
explanation: Total: 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 10 + 3 = 33, one short. Selenium is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p4 (34 electrons); the student's version belongs to arsenic.

q: A neutral atom has the configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p3. Which element is it?
explanation: 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 3 = 15 electrons. A neutral atom with 15 electrons has Z = 15: phosphorus.

q: Which electron configuration belongs to the element marked X on the periodic table outline?
explanation: X is in row 4, group 15 (arsenic, Z = 33). After [Ar], read across row 4: 4s2, 3d10, 4p3. [Ar] 4s2 3d10 4p3. Check: 18 + 2 + 10 + 3 = 33.

q: Chloride is the main negative ion in blood. How many valence electrons does a chlorine atom have?
explanation: Cl is in group 17: 17 − 10 = 7 valence electrons, the 3s2 3p5 electrons of its highest shell. Gaining 1 gives Cl− an octet.

q: Selenium is [Ar] 4s2 3d10 4p4. How many valence electrons does it have?
explanation: Selenium's highest shell is n = 4, holding 4s2 4p4: 6 valence electrons. This matches group 16: 16 − 10 = 6.

q: Aluminum is in group 13. Use the octet rule to predict the ion it forms.
explanation: Group 13: 13 − 10 = 3 valence electrons. Aluminum is a metal and loses all 3, forming Al3+ with neon's configuration (10 electrons).

q: Why does oxygen form O2− rather than O6+?
key: Gaining 2 electrons to reach an octet is much easier than losing all 6 valence electrons.
wrong: Oxygen has 2 valence electrons, and it gains 2 more.
Oxygen always loses electrons, because it is a nonmetal.
O2− has the same number of protons as neon.
explanation: Oxygen has 6 valence electrons. Gaining 2 reaches an octet (neon's configuration) in 2 steps; losing 6 would take 6. So oxygen forms O2−, oxide.

q: Why are the noble gases, such as neon and argon, so unreactive?
key: Their valence shells are already full (an octet, or 2 electrons for helium).
wrong: They have no valence electrons at all.
Their atoms are too large to react.
They have only one valence electron, which they hold very tightly.
explanation: Group 18 atoms already have a full valence shell: ns2 np6, an octet (helium: 1s2). They have no electrons to lose easily and no room to gain more, so they barely react.

q: Four main-group elements are marked on the periodic table outline. Which one is most likely to form a 2− ion?
explanation: A 2− ion means gaining 2 electrons, which fits an atom with 6 valence electrons: group 16. C is in group 16. A (group 2) forms 2+, B (group 17) forms 1−, and D (group 18) forms no ion.

q: Which pair of elements would you expect to have the most similar chemical properties?
explanation: Elements in the same group have the same valence configuration. Sodium and potassium are both group 1 (ns1), so both lose one electron to form Na+ and K+.

q: IV fluid labels give ion amounts in milliequivalents (mEq), a unit that accounts for charge. For which ion does 1 mmol equal 2 mEq?
explanation: Milliequivalents = millimoles × size of the charge. Group 2 calcium loses 2 valence electrons to form Ca2+, so 1 mmol = 2 mEq. Na+, K+ and Cl− each have a charge of size 1. (Context only; this is not dosing guidance.)

q: In an electron-dot (Lewis) symbol, how many dots are drawn around the symbol for nitrogen?
explanation: Dot symbols show valence electrons. Nitrogen (group 15) has 2s2 2p3: 5 dots.

q: Na+ has the same electron configuration as a neon atom. Which statement is true?
key: Na+ is still sodium, because it still has 11 protons.
wrong: Na+ has turned into a neon atom.
explanation: Na+ has 11 protons and 10 electrons. It is isoelectronic with neon (10 electrons) but still sodium, because the proton count did not change.

q: Which of these group 1 atoms has the largest atomic radius?
explanation: Going down a group adds a shell, so atomic radius increases: Li < Na < K < Rb. Rb is the largest.

q: Rank Al, P and Cl in order of increasing atomic radius.
explanation: Across a period, the nuclear charge grows while electrons go into the same shell, so atomic radius decreases left to right. Increasing radius: Cl < P < Al.

q: Which row-3 element has the highest first ionization energy: Na, Si, S or Ar?
explanation: Across a row, ionization energy increases. The noble gas, Ar, has the highest in row 3; Na has the lowest.

q: Which halogen has the lowest first ionization energy?
explanation: Going down a group, valence electrons are in higher shells, farther out and more shielded, so ionization energy decreases: F > Cl > Br > I. Iodine is lowest.

q: Which is larger, a chlorine atom (Cl) or a chloride ion (Cl−), and why?
key: Cl−, because it has one more electron than protons, so its electrons repel each other more and the cloud spreads out.
wrong: Cl, because the ion has gained a proton.
Cl, because adding an electron pulls the cloud in tighter.
They are the same size, because both have 17 protons.
explanation: Anions are larger than their atoms. Cl− has 18 electrons and 17 protons; the extra electron increases repulsion and the electron cloud spreads out.

q: Na+ and K+ both carry a 1+ charge, but potassium channels in nerve cells sort them by size. Which ion is larger?
key: K+, because its outermost electrons are in a higher shell (shell 3) than those of Na+ (shell 2).
wrong: Na+, because sodium comes first in the group.
They are the same size, because they have the same charge.
Na+, because it has fewer protons pulling on its electrons.
explanation: Down a group, ions get larger just as atoms do. K+ (18 electrons, outer shell 3) is larger than Na+ (10 electrons, outer shell 2). Channel proteins use this size difference to pass K+ selectively.

q: Which element has the most metallic character?
explanation: Metallic character increases toward the lower left, where atoms are large and ionization energies are low. Of these, Cs is farthest down and to the left.

q: Four elements are marked on the periodic table outline. Which one has the largest atomic radius?
explanation: Atomic radius increases down a group and decreases across a row, so the largest atom is the one farthest down and left: B (row 4, group 1, potassium).

q: Four elements are marked on the periodic table outline. Which one has the highest first ionization energy?
explanation: Ionization energy increases up a group and across a row, so it is highest toward the upper right: A (row 2, group 17, fluorine). D (rubidium) is lowest.

q: Why do atoms get smaller from left to right across a period, even though each one has more electrons?
key: Each step adds a proton while the new electron goes into the same shell, so the stronger nuclear pull draws the valence electrons closer.
wrong: Each step adds a new shell, which squeezes the electrons together.
Electrons repel each other less when there are more of them.
The atoms on the right lose electrons more easily.
explanation: Across a period, every element adds one proton, while its electrons stay in the same shell. Same-shell electrons shield each other poorly, so the effective nuclear charge increases and pulls the valence electrons in.

q: Aluminum nitrate has the formula Al(NO3)3. How many oxygen atoms are in one formula unit?
explanation: In Al(NO3)3, the subscript 3 outside the parentheses multiplies everything inside: 3 N atoms and 3 × 3 = 9 O atoms, plus 1 Al atom.

q: Ammonium sulfate, (NH4)2SO4, is a nitrogen fertilizer used on many Valley farms. How many atoms in total are in one formula unit?
explanation: N: 2; H: 4 × 2 = 8; S: 1; O: 4. Total = 15 atoms. The sulfate group is outside the parentheses, so it is counted once.

q: Tooth enamel is mostly hydroxyapatite, Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2. How many oxygen atoms are in one formula unit?
explanation: Phosphate: 6 × 4 = 24 O. Hydroxide: 2 × 1 = 2 O. Total = 26 O atoms (along with 10 Ca, 6 P and 2 H).

q: During exercise, muscle cells break down glucose, C6H12O6. How many carbon atoms are in 2 C6H12O6 (two glucose molecules)?
explanation: One C6H12O6 molecule has 6 C atoms, so 2 C6H12O6 has 2 × 6 = 12 C atoms (and 24 H, 12 O).

q: Which of these elements exists as a diatomic molecule (two atoms bonded together) when it is uncombined?
explanation: The diatomic elements are H2, N2, O2, F2, Cl2, Br2 and I2. Of these choices, only iodine (I2) is on the list.

q: A patient receives supplemental oxygen from a tank. The gas in the tank is uncombined (elemental) oxygen. Which formula represents it?
explanation: Oxygen is one of the seven diatomic elements, so the gas in the tank is O2. Writing O instead of O2 is a common mistake.

q: Which compound is ionic even though every element in it is a nonmetal?
explanation: A formula that starts with a metal or with NH4 is ionic. NH4Cl contains ammonium ions and chloride ions, so it is ionic even though N, H and Cl are all nonmetals.

q: Which of these is an acid?
explanation: Acids have formulas that start with H and release H+ in water. HBr(aq) is hydrobromic acid. A formula that ends in OH after a metal is a hydroxide, not an acid.

q: Which of these compounds is molecular?
explanation: Molecular compounds contain only nonmetals. Na, Zn and Al are metals, so their oxides are ionic; N2O contains only nitrogen and oxygen, so it is molecular.

q: Magnesium hydroxide, Mg(OH)2, is the active ingredient in milk of magnesia. How is it classified?
key: Ionic, because its formula starts with a metal
wrong: An acid, because its formula contains H
Molecular, because O and H are nonmetals
explanation: The formula starts with the metal Mg, so it is ionic: one Mg2+ ion and two OH− (hydroxide) ions. A formula that ends in OH after a metal is a hydroxide, not an acid.

q: What is the formula of the ionic compound formed by calcium and nitrogen?
explanation: Ca2+ and N3−. Swap-drop gives Ca3N2; 3 × 2 = 6 and 2 × 3 = 6, so the charges cancel and no reducing is needed.

q: What is the formula of barium sulfide?
explanation: Ba2+ and S2−: swap-drop gives Ba2S2, which reduces to BaS. Ions with charges 2+ and 2− always combine 1 : 1.

q: Dental air-abrasion units blast tiny particles of aluminum oxide at a tooth surface. What is the formula of aluminum oxide?
explanation: Al3+ and O2−. Swap-drop: Al2O3. The 2 and 3 have no common factor, so the formula is already reduced.

q: What is the formula of magnesium phosphate?
explanation: Mg2+ and PO43−. Swap-drop: 3 Mg and 2 PO4, written Mg3(PO4)2. Check: 3(2+) + 2(3−) = 0.

q: Lithium carbonate is a medication used to treat bipolar disorder. What is its formula?
explanation: Li+ and CO32−: swap-drop gives Li2CO3. Check: 2(1+) + (2−) = 0. (Context only; not dosing information.)

q: What is the formula of ammonium sulfide?
explanation: NH4+ and S2−. Swap-drop gives 2 ammonium and 1 sulfide: (NH4)2S. Check: 2(1+) + (2−) = 0.

q: Chromium(III) ions combine with hydroxide ions. What is the formula of the compound?
explanation: Cr3+ and OH−. Swap-drop gives 1 Cr and 3 OH: Cr(OH)3. Check: (3+) + 3(1−) = 0.

q: What is the charge on each cobalt ion in Co2O3?
explanation: Total negative charge: 3 × (2−) = 6−. The two Co ions must carry 6+ together, so each is Co3+. Check: 2(3+) + 3(2−) = 0.

q: What is the charge on each iron ion in Fe3(PO4)2?
explanation: Total negative charge: 2 × (3−) = 6−. Three Fe ions carry 6+ together, so each is Fe2+. Check: 3(2+) + 2(3−) = 0.

q: Calcium oxalate, CaC2O4, is the most common compound in kidney stones. The calcium ion is Ca2+. What is the charge of the oxalate ion?
explanation: Ca2+ + oxalate = 0, so oxalate is 2−: C2O42−, as on the green sheet.

q: The table pairs each cation with each anion and gives the formula of the compound they form. Which formula belongs in the cell marked ?
explanation: Al3+ and PO43−: swap-drop gives Al3(PO4)3, which reduces to AlPO4. No parentheses are needed for one phosphate.

q: For a barium swallow X-ray, a patient drinks a suspension of barium sulfate. What is its formula?
explanation: Ba2+ and SO42−: swap-drop gives Ba2(SO4)2, which reduces to BaSO4. Barium sulfate is almost insoluble, which is why it can be swallowed safely while soluble barium compounds are poisonous.

q: In an infant's body, nitrate from well water can be converted to the nitrite ion. What is the formula of the nitrite ion?
explanation: Nitrate is NO3−; -ite means one fewer O with the same charge, so nitrite is NO2−.

q: What is the name of the ion ClO2−?
explanation: Chlorine oxyanions: ClO4− perchlorate, ClO3− chlorate, ClO2− chlorite, ClO− hypochlorite. The charge tells you it is an ion, not the molecule ClO2.

q: Iodate is IO3−. What is the formula of the periodate ion?
explanation: Per-...-ate = one more O than -ate, same charge. Iodate is IO3−, so periodate is IO4−.

q: Sulfate is SO42−. What is the formula of the sulfite ion?
explanation: Sulfate SO42− loses one O to give sulfite, SO32−. The charge stays 2−.

q: What is the formula of the hydrogen phosphate ion?
explanation: PO43− + H+ gives HPO42−, hydrogen phosphate. Each added H+ lowers the negative charge by one.

q: An arterial blood gas report lists the level of HCO3− in the blood. What is the name of this ion?
explanation: Remove the H+ and you have carbonate, CO32−. With one H added, the ion is hydrogen carbonate, also called bicarbonate, the "bicarb" on a blood gas report.

q: IV potassium phosphate contains the dihydrogen phosphate ion. What is its formula?
explanation: PO43− + 2 H+ gives H2PO4−, dihydrogen phosphate. (Context only; not dosing information.)

q: Which pair of ions has the same charge?
explanation: Changing -ate to -ite (one fewer O) never changes the charge, so nitrate (NO3−) and nitrite (NO2−) are both 1−. Adding H+ or switching to an -ide ion does change it.

q: What is the formula of the acetate ion?
explanation: Acetate is C2H3O2−. Oxalate, C2O42−, is easy to mix up with it.

q: The table lists the bromine oxyanions. Which name belongs in the cell marked ?
explanation: BrO4− perbromate, BrO3− bromate, BrO2− bromite, BrO− hypobromite. Bromine follows the same pattern as chlorine.

q: What is the name of K2S?
explanation: Cation name + anion name: potassium sulfide. Group 1 metals never get Roman numerals, and ionic names never use prefixes.

q: What is the name of AgCl?
explanation: Ag is a fixed-charge metal (Ag+), so the name is simply silver chloride.

q: What is the name of Cu2O?
explanation: O2− = 2−, shared by 2 Cu, so each is Cu+: copper(I) oxide (older name cuprous oxide). The Roman numeral is the charge, not the subscript.

q: What is the name of Co(NO3)2?
explanation: 2 NO3− = 2−, so cobalt is Co2+: cobalt(II) nitrate (older name cobaltous nitrate).

q: What is the name of Cr2(SO4)3?
explanation: 3 × (2−) = 6−, over 2 Cr ions = 3+ each: chromium(III) sulfate (older name chromic sulfate).

q: Ferrous sulfate is a common iron supplement. What is its formula?
explanation: Ferrous = iron(II) = Fe2+. Fe2+ and SO42− give FeSO4. (Context only; not dosing information.)

q: Older labels use -ous and -ic names. What is the older name of CuSO4?
explanation: SO42− = 2−, so Cu2+: copper(II) sulfate, or with the older name, cupric sulfate.

q: What is the formula of mercurous nitrate?
explanation: Mercurous = mercury(I) = Hg22+. With NO3−: Hg2(NO3)2. Each Hg is 1+, but the ion is the pair.

q: Household bleach is a solution of sodium hypochlorite. What is its formula?
explanation: Hypochlorite is ClO−; with Na+ the formula is NaClO. Never mix bleach with acids or ammonia.

q: Ammonium nitrate, NH4NO3, is a Valley fertilizer. A student writes four names for it. Which is correct?
explanation: NH4+ + NO3− = ammonium nitrate. Watch the spelling: ammonium (the ion), not ammonia (the molecule).

q: Humidity-indicator cards turn pink when they absorb water to form CoCl2·6H2O. What is its name?
explanation: 2 Cl− = 2−, so Co2+: cobalt(II) chloride. Six H2O = hexahydrate: cobalt(II) chloride hexahydrate.

q: Zinc sulfate heptahydrate is sprayed on some Valley orchards to correct zinc deficiency. What is its formula?
explanation: Zinc sulfate is ZnSO4 (Zn2+, SO42−); hepta = 7, so ZnSO4·7H2O.

q: A student wrote the names in the table. Which row is named correctly?
explanation: A: sodium oxide (no prefixes). B: iron(III) chloride is correct. C: calcium chloride (no numeral). D: lead(IV) oxide.

q: Calcium supplements and bone mineral contain Ca3(PO4)2. What is its name?
explanation: Ca2+ + PO43−: calcium phosphate, with no prefixes and no Roman numeral.

q: What is the name of S2Cl2?
explanation: Molecular: prefix + first element, prefix + second element with -ide. 2 S, 2 Cl: disulfur dichloride.

q: Eye surgeons sometimes place a bubble of sulfur hexafluoride gas inside the eye after retina repair. What is its formula?
explanation: Sulfur (no prefix, 1 S) hexa- (6) fluoride: SF6.

q: In neonatal intensive care, respiratory therapists can deliver inhaled NO to some newborns. What is the systematic name of NO?
explanation: Nitrogen monoxide: no mono- on the first element; mono- + oxide (with the o dropped) on the second. Its common name is nitric oxide.

q: On hot days the brown haze over the San Joaquin Valley includes nitrogen dioxide. What is its formula?
explanation: Nitrogen (1 N) di- (2) oxide: NO2, a neutral molecule. Do not confuse it with NO2−, the nitrite ion.

q: Which formula and name are matched correctly?
explanation: N2O4: dinitrogen tetroxide is correct. NO2 is nitrogen dioxide, CO is carbon monoxide, SiO2 is silicon dioxide.

q: A student names CaF2 "calcium difluoride" and SF2 "sulfur fluoride." Which pair of corrected names is right?
explanation: Ionic CaF2: calcium fluoride (no prefix). Molecular SF2: sulfur difluoride (prefix required). Same F count, different rules.

q: What is the name of PBr3?
explanation: One P, three Br: phosphorus tribromide.

q: Why do names of molecular compounds use Greek prefixes, when names of ionic compounds do not?
key: Nonmetals can combine in more than one ratio, and there are no ion charges to fix the ratio, so the name must count the atoms.
wrong: Molecular compounds are made of ions with larger charges, so the prefixes give the charges.
Prefixes are used whenever a compound contains oxygen.
Molecular compounds always contain exactly two atoms, so the prefixes are only for spelling.
explanation: Ionic ratios are fixed by charges, so the name does not need to count ions. Molecular compounds have no charges, and the same two nonmetals can form several molecules (CO, CO2), so prefixes count the atoms.

q: What is the name of I2O5?
explanation: 2 I, 5 O: diiodine pentoxide. Before oxide, a vowel at the end of a prefix is usually dropped (pentoxide, monoxide).

q: The common name ammonia refers to which formula?
explanation: Ammonia is NH3. Adding H+ gives the ammonium ion, NH4+.

q: What is the name of HI(aq)?
explanation: The anion is iodide, I−, an -ide ion, so the acid is hydro- + iod + -ic: hydroiodic acid.

q: What is the name of H2S(aq)?
explanation: Sulfide (-ide) becomes hydro-...-ic: hydrosulfuric acid. Sulfuric acid, H2SO4, is a different compound.

q: Car batteries contain H2SO4. What is the name of this acid?
explanation: SO42− is sulfate; -ate → -ic: sulfuric acid. Oxyacids never get hydro-.

q: What is the name of HBrO2?
explanation: BrO2− = bromite; -ite → -ous: bromous acid.

q: Many colas contain phosphoric acid. What is its formula?
explanation: Phosphoric ← phosphate, PO43−; 3 H+: H3PO4.

q: In water, bleach forms hypochlorous acid, which kills bacteria. What is its formula?
explanation: Hypochlorous ← hypochlorite, ClO−; one H+: HClO. Prefixes such as hypo- and per- stay in acid names.

q: What is the name of HIO4?
explanation: IO4− = periodate; -ate → -ic, prefix kept: periodic acid (per-iodic, nothing to do with the periodic table).

q: Vinegar is about 5% acetic acid in water. What is the formula of acetic acid?
explanation: Acetic ← acetate, C2H3O2−; add one H+: HC2H3O2 (also written CH3COOH).

q: Carbon dioxide dissolved in blood forms H2CO3. What is its name?
explanation: CO32− = carbonate; -ate → -ic: carbonic acid. It releases H+ and bicarbonate in blood.

q: The table shows anions and the acids made from them. Which name belongs in the cell marked ?
explanation: Sulfite gave sulfurous acid, so chlorite gives chlorous acid, HClO2.
